Meta's gearing up for a stock sale.

On Monday, Meta launched a plan to raise up to $95 billion in stock, upsized Tuesday to $97.5 billion. Naturally, Nvidia and AMD, two of Meta's biggest chip suppliers, said they were buying. Nvidia would invest $3 billion and AMD $1 billion. Just 96% of the raise to go as the circle in circular finance continues to spin.

Meta carried about $115 billion in debt and lease obligations as of September 30, per its quarterly filing, within $206.45 billion in total liabilities. Its future commitments dwarf both. Bloomberg reported on October 22 that Meta's lease and contract commitments hit about $825 billion, up from nearly $700 billion in July. That total includes $355.7 billion in leases not yet on the balance sheet, per the filing. Nikkei Asia put the figure at $420 billion in late July.

Capex keeps climbing on top of that. Meta narrowed its 2026 guidance last week to $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the floor and implying $49 billion to $59 billion in Q4 spending alone. The combined weight likely forced Meta's hand: it issued more stock.

One stock. Nvidia-level potential. 30M+ investors trust Moby to find it first. Get the pick. Tap here.

At the same time, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he would help Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg out with $3 billion, the companies said. Meta plans to deploy more Nvidia Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs to support Muse, Meta's AI agent. Muse launched last month and is third on the U.S. free iPhone chart as of October 26, behind Vinted, a secondhand store app, and TikTok Pro. It's ahead of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

The good thing about issuing new common shares is Meta doesn't have to pay anything back or pay interest. That said, $12.5 billion of preferred pays a 6.5% dividend. The bad thing is shareholders get diluted by about 5.5% if the full plan sells, per a StockTitan estimate. EPS is also going to take a hit if Meta can't pump its profits.

But that's the price Big Tech and the hyperscalers feel is worth paying to guarantee their slice of the AI industry. If they don't grab it now, someone else will.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) has had an incredible year as a stock. It's up around 140% so far in 2026, good enough to be in the top 10 best-performing stocks in the S&P 500. It's also crushing rival Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), which is only up around 13%.

However, what's in the past is in the past. It's time for investors to look to the future and see what to do with AMD stock. I'm currently not an AMD shareholder (to my error), but if I were, would it be time to hold or sell the stock? Or should I take a look at opening up a position?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
AMD's growth case is looking up

At the start of the AI race, AMD's technology was lagging behind Nvidia's. As a result, it lost a ton of early market share to its rival, Nvidia. However, AMD has started to catch up and has made several deals with AI hyperscalers, like OpenAI, to supply them with computing power. This has led to strong growth, with data center revenue rising 107% year over year in the second quarter to $6.7 billion.

AMD also has significant consumer and embedded processor segments, so its overall growth rate in Q2 was 52%, but the biggest improvement in AMD has come from its profit margin.

AMD Profit Margin (Quarterly) data by YCharts.

AMD's profit margin has improved steadily and continues to get stronger. If AMD can keep this trend up, the future looks very bright for the company.

Wall Street analysts expect AMD's growth rate to take a step back next quarter, and only rise to 41%. However, they expect 57% growth in the fourth quarter, and in 2027, they expect 75% growth. That's spectacular, and makes investors wonder if AMD stock could repeat in 2027.

That's the bull case, but the bear case is much more rooted in reality.

AMD's stock has already priced in future growth

I am not denying that AMD has great growth prospects. I think that it will have a phenomenal year as a company in 2027. The issue is that all this growth is already priced into AMD's stock. If you value the stock using this year's and next year's earnings estimates, it reveals that AMD is a very expensive stock.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

AMD trades for a very pricey 68 times forward earnings and 33 times next year's earnings. For reference, rival Nvidia trades at 27 times trailing earnings right now. That means that there is about a year and a half worth of growth priced into AMD's stock, which could affect future returns.

title: Should You Buy AMD Stock Before Nov. 3?

Should You Buy AMD Stock Before Nov. 3?

As artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers race to build data centers, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) is swiftly emerging as a formidable competitor to GPU powerhouse Nvidia.

As of this writing (Oct. 28), AMD stock has skyrocketed 164% in 2026, handily outpacing both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite, which have gained 12.9% and 13.8%, respectively. The company is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Nov. 3.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Considering shares have already enjoyed a sizable rally, should investors buy AMD stock before the upcoming announcement, or has Wall Street gotten ahead of itself? Let's take a closer look.

What does Wall Street expect for AMD earnings?

AMD's second-quarter financial results illustrated how the company is expanding. Total revenue increased 50% year over year to $11.5 billion, while adjusted earnings per share (EPS) reached $1.66. More importantly, AMD's data center business generated $6.7 billion in revenue, representing 107% growth year over year.

Naturally, this momentum raised expectations for the upcoming third-quarter report. According to Wall Street's consensus estimates, analysts anticipate AMD to generate $13.1 billion in revenue and EPS of $1.93.

Here's the challenge: Strong earnings don't automatically translate into a higher stock price. When a stock has already appreciated substantially, investors tend to expect more than simply meeting consensus estimates. AMD will need to deliver an impressive earnings beat and raise its fourth-quarter outlook to justify another rally.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
What tailwinds does AMD have?

AMD's Instinct AI accelerators are gaining traction among cloud computing companies seeking alternatives to Nvidia's chips. The company recently introduced its MI400-series accelerators, including the MI455X, designed to handle increasingly demanding AI training and inference workloads.

Meanwhile, its Helios rack-scale platform combines advanced GPUs, processors, networking, and software into one integrated AI computing system. Customers and partners include Microsoft, Meta Platforms, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

Beyond GPUs, AMD's Epyc server processors are another growth opportunity. These chips power data centers and compete with Intel's server CPUs, allowing AMD to benefit from broader AI infrastructure demand beyond accelerators.

title: Advanced Micro Devices vs. Dell Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Advanced Micro Devices vs. Dell Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Mike Schwenk, The Motley Fool

DELL
MSFT
SONY
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

As the artificial intelligence era moves from experimentation to massive infrastructure deployment, investors are comparing Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) and Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) to find the best way to profit.

While both companies are central to modern computing, they serve different functions. One designs the advanced chips that power complex calculations, while the other assembles the servers and storage systems that businesses rely on. Understanding their distinct business models is key to choosing the right stock.

The case for Advanced Micro Devices

Advanced Micro Devices designs high-performance, adaptive computing products for a wide range of customers across the cloud, embedded systems, and gaming markets.

The company is a key player in the semiconductor sector, providing essential processors for data centers and personal computers. Its semi-custom chips power the Sony (NYSE:SONY) PlayStation 5 and the Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) Xbox Series consoles, according to its latest annual report.

In October 2025, the company also entered into a multiyear agreement with OpenAI to deploy up to 6 gigawatts of AMD GPUs, and in February 2026, it signed a similar 6-gigawatt agreement with Meta Platforms(NASDAQ:META).

Both customers received warrants to buy up to 160 million AMD shares each at $0.01 per share, with vesting contingent on purchases and stock price milestones being met.

AMD's annual report says it depends on a small number of customers for a substantial portion of its business, and one customer accounted for 11% of its receivables at the end of 2025. This level of customer concentration adds risk to the business.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 27, 2025, revenue reached nearly $34.6 billion, up about 34.3% from the prior fiscal year. Strong demand for its AI infrastructure and data center products drove this increase.

The company reported net income of roughly $4.3 billion for the same period. This marks a substantial improvement in profitability as the company scales its newest chip architectures.

Growth has accelerated since. In the second quarter of 2026, ended June 27, revenue rose 50% year over year to $11.5 billion and net income reached $2.3 billion, with data center revenue up 107% to $6.7 billion.

Management guided third-quarter revenue to approximately $13 billion, plus or minus $300 million. On Sept. 28, 2026, AMD announced an agreement to acquire World Labs, the spatial-intelligence lab led by Fei-Fei Li, for approximately $8.2 billion in AMD stock, with closing expected by the end of 2026.

The pushback against OKX and ICE's tokenized stock venue now includes the biggest bank in the U.S.

JPMorgan Chase, Coca-Cola, and Dell Technologies are among seven companies added to OKXICE TSV's list of objecting issuers in a notice dated Tuesday. Advanced Micro Devices, Adobe, Applied Materials, and Sandisk round out the group. The additions bring the total to 33, up from 26 a day earlier.

Myriad: Which company will IPO next? Click to make your prediction.

The list has grown quickly. It stood at nine on Oct. 15, 16 on Oct. 19, and 22 on Oct. 23. Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Intel, and Oracle. JPMorgan is the third major bank to object, after Goldman and Wells Fargo.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. The objection applies only to that venue. The notices haven't disclosed the companies' reasons.

OKXICE's original Oct. 4 notice proposed 63 tokenized stocks from 62 companies, and several objectors, including Wells Fargo and Arm, weren't on that initial roster. Some of the biggest names, including Nvidia, Tesla, Apple, and Amazon, haven't objected so far.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7. Trades would run through permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC. Earlier notices warned that it's uncertain whether tokenized shares in self-custodied wallets would be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation if the tokenizer's broker-dealer failed.

OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before announcing the 24/7 venue this month. Nasdaq, which won SEC approval for its own tokenized securities pilot, has said it will opt its shares out of the exemption.

JPMorgan, Coca-Cola Join Pushback Against OKX-ICE Tokenized Stock Trading

JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: $JPM), Coca-Cola (NYSE: $KO), and Dell Technologies (NYSE: $DELL) and four other companies have also objected to plans by crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange owner Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: $ICE) to offer tokenized versions of their shares.

An updated notice dated October 27 added JPMorgan, Coca-Cola, Dell, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: $AMD), Adobe (NASDAQ: $ADBE), Applied Materials (NASDAQ: $AMAT) and Sandisk (NASDAQ: $SNDK) to the list.

The seven companies were among the 62 firms originally notified by OKXICE, bringing the number of disclosed objections to 33, meaning about 48% of the initial roster has now objected.

The objections come amid growing caution among publicly traded companies as crypto platforms explore ways to bring traditional stocks onto blockchains.

OKXICE announced its plans on Oct. 4, proposing round-the-clock trading of tokenized US stocks through permissioned Uniswap (CRYPTO: $UNI) v4 liquidity pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. Transactions would settle in stablecoins, including USDC (CRYPTO: $USDC).

The venue would operate under the US Securities and Exchange Commission's five-year "Innovation Exemption," which allows qualifying platforms to test blockchain-based stock trading using automated market makers.

Companies have 30 days after notification to object to the inclusion of their shares. A written objection prevents the venue from offering that company's stock, although it does not automatically exclude the shares from other platforms.

The objection list has expanded rapidly, growing from nine companies on Oct. 15 to 16 on Oct. 19 and 22 on Oct. 23. Earlier objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Intel and Oracle.

Several major companies, including Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA), Tesla (NASDAQ: $TSLA), Apple (NASDAQ: $AAPL), and Amazon (NASDAQ: $AMZN), have not objected so far. Meanwhile, Nasdaq has said it will exclude its own shares from the SEC's exemption-based framework as it explores tokenized securities.
